domanda: During a design review, a colleague asks why Azure requires you to select a location when you create a resource group, given that the resources inside the group can be deployed to entirely different regions. Which statement correctly explains the purpose of the resource group location?
opzione_a: The location determines the region where the resource group stores the metadata about its resources.
opzione_b: The location restricts the resources in the resource group to that region only.
opzione_c: The location determines the region whose meter rates are used to bill all resources in the resource group.
opzione_d: The location defines the paired region to which Azure automatically replicates all resources in the resource group for disaster recovery.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn states that the resource group stores metadata about its resources, so specifying a location for the resource group specifies where that metadata is stored. This matters for compliance and data residency, and control plane operations for the group are routed through that location. Wrong: b - the documentation explicitly says the resources in a resource group can be located in different regions than the resource group (using the same location is only a recommendation). Wrong: c - billing rates are determined by the region of each individual resource and its meters, not by the resource group's location; a resource group is not a billing construct. Wrong: d - a resource group location does not create replication or disaster recovery for the resources it contains; ARM only fails over control plane requests for the resource group's metadata to a secondary region, which is not the same as replicating the resources.
tags: resource group, region, metadata, azure resource manager, governance

domanda: A colleague starts a move operation to relocate several virtual machines from a resource group named RG-Prod to a resource group named RG-Archive in the same subscription. While the move is running, another engineer reports that she cannot resize a virtual machine that is not part of the move but resides in RG-Prod. What is the expected behavior during a resource move operation?
opzione_a: Both the source and the destination resource groups are locked, so resources in them cannot be created, deleted, or updated, but existing resources keep running without downtime.
opzione_b: Only the source resource group is locked; the destination resource group remains fully writable until the move completes.
opzione_c: The resources included in the move are automatically stopped and deallocated for the duration of the move, and other resources in the resource group are unaffected.
opzione_d: A read-only lock is automatically applied at the subscription scope, blocking all write operations across every resource group in the subscription.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn states that during the move operation both the source and target resource groups are locked, so you cannot create, delete, or update resources within these resource groups while the move is in progress; however, existing resources remain fully operational and services relying on them experience no downtime. The lock can last up to four hours, although most moves finish sooner. This is exactly why resizing a VM in RG-Prod fails. Wrong: b - the lock is applied to both the source and the destination resource groups, not just the source, and neither can participate in another move simultaneously. Wrong: c - moving a resource does not stop or deallocate it; the documentation is explicit that the VM continues to operate normally and dependent services see no downtime. Also, the lock affects the whole resource group, not only the resources being moved. Wrong: d - the automatic lock is scoped to the two resource groups involved, not to the entire subscription. (Separately, a manually created read-only lock on the source or destination blocks the move from happening at all.)
tags: move resources, resource group, lock, azure resource manager, troubleshooting

domanda: Your team is consolidating resources into a new resource group. Which resource type CANNOT be moved to a different resource group?
spiegazione: Correct: d. In the Azure resource types for move operations reference, Microsoft.Network/applicationGateways is listed as No for resource group move, No for subscription move, and No for region move. An application gateway must be re-created in the target resource group instead. Wrong: a - Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts supports both resource group and subscription moves. Wrong: b - Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups is listed as Yes for resource group move, Yes for subscription move, and even supports region move via Azure Resource Mover. Wrong: c - Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults is listed as Yes for both resource group and subscription moves (region move is not supported, but the question asks about a resource group move).
tags: move resources, move support, application gateway, resource group, limitations

domanda: Contoso is consolidating workloads and needs to move a virtual machine and its dependent resources from a subscription named Sub-Legacy to a subscription named Sub-Corp. You must ensure the move operation succeeds on the first attempt. Which conditions must be satisfied before you start the move? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Both the source and the destination subscriptions must exist within the same Microsoft Entra tenant.
opzione_b: The destination subscription must be registered for the resource provider of each resource type being moved.
opzione_c: The resource and its dependent resources must be located in the same resource group and must be moved together in the same operation.
opzione_d: The source resource group and the destination resource group must be created in the same Azure region.
opzione_e: All existing Azure role assignments on the moved resources are automatically re-created in the destination subscription, so no post-move action is required.
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, c. The Microsoft Learn checklist for moving resources states that (a) the source and destination subscriptions must exist within the same Microsoft Entra tenant - if the tenant IDs differ you must first transfer billing ownership or associate the subscription with the target tenant; (b) the destination subscription must be registered for the resource provider of the resource you're moving, otherwise you receive an error stating the subscription isn't registered for a resource type; and (c) for a move across subscriptions, the resource and its dependent resources must be located in the same resource group and be moved together - a VM with managed disks requires the VM, the disks, and the other dependent resources to move in one operation, otherwise you get MissingMoveDependentResources. Wrong: d - there is no requirement that the source and destination resource groups share a region. Moving a resource only changes its associated resource group and does not alter the physical region of the resource; a region change requires Azure Resource Mover instead. Wrong: e - the opposite is documented: if you move a resource with an active Azure role assignment, the role assignment does not move and becomes orphaned. You must create the role assignment again after the move, and Microsoft recommends removing the orphaned assignment before the move.
tags: move resources, subscription move, entra tenant, resource provider, dependent resources, rbac

domanda: While planning a management group hierarchy for a large enterprise, you need to document the maximum nesting supported. Up to how many levels of depth can a management group tree support, excluding the root management group level and the subscription level?
spiegazione: Correct: b. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about management groups' states that a management group tree can support up to six levels of depth, and that this limit does not include the root level or the subscription level. Wrong: a - 4 is a commonly cited Cloud Adoption Framework design recommendation for practical hierarchy depth, but it is not the platform limit. Wrong: c and d - 8 and 10 exceed the documented limit; the other published management group limits are 10,000 management groups per single directory and one parent per management group or subscription.
tags: management groups, hierarchy, depth, limits, governance

domanda: An auditor asks you to explain how the top of your organization's Azure governance hierarchy works. Which statement about the root management group is TRUE?
opzione_a: The root management group's ID is the same value as the Microsoft Entra tenant ID, and unlike other management groups it cannot be moved or deleted.
opzione_b: The root management group can be deleted after all child management groups and subscriptions have been moved out of it.
opzione_c: Users who are assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID are granted the Owner role on the root management group by default.
opzione_d: You can create additional root management groups in a directory to keep production and development hierarchies completely separate.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about the root management group' states that the ID is the same value as the Microsoft Entra tenant ID, that the default display name is 'Tenant root group', and that the root management group can't be moved or deleted, unlike other management groups. Wrong: b - the root management group can never be deleted, regardless of whether it still has children. (The rule that a management group must have no child management groups or subscriptions before deletion applies to non-root management groups.) Wrong: c - this is the classic misconception. No one has default access to the root management group. Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only users who can elevate themselves to gain access, which assigns them the User Access Administrator role at root scope; only after elevating can they assign roles such as Owner. Wrong: d - each directory has a single top-level root management group, and all subscriptions and management groups are within a single hierarchy in each directory. This single hierarchy exists specifically so that global access and policy assignments cannot be bypassed.
tags: management groups, root management group, tenant root group, entra id, governance

domanda: Fabrikam is designing a management group hierarchy for its Microsoft Entra tenant and needs to record the supported platform limits and default behaviors in a design document. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of management groups in a single directory: [1000 | 10000 | 50000]
opzione_b: Maximum levels of management group depth, excluding the root level and the subscription level: [4 | 6 | 8]
opzione_c: Maximum number of parent management groups that a subscription can have: [1 | 2 | Unlimited]
opzione_d: Default parent of a newly created subscription: [Root management group | No parent until assigned | The most recently created management group]
spiegazione: Correct values: 10000 / 6 / 1 / Root management group. Microsoft Learn's 'Important facts about management groups' states that a single directory can support 10,000 management groups; that a management group tree can support up to six levels of depth, not including the root level or the subscription level; and that each management group and subscription can support only one parent (while each management group can have many children). The 'Important facts about the root management group' section states that new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group when they're created, which is also why you don't need permissions on the root management group to move an item into or out of it. Wrong values: 1000 and 50000 are not the documented directory limit. 4 is a common Cloud Adoption Framework design guideline rather than the platform maximum, and 8 exceeds the limit. 2 and Unlimited contradict the single-parent rule that keeps all subscriptions and management groups within one hierarchy per directory. 'No parent until assigned' and 'The most recently created management group' contradict the documented default landing spot for new subscriptions.
tags: management groups, limits, hierarchy, root management group, subscriptions

domanda:
Anna is assigned the Global Administrator role in your Microsoft Entra tenant, but she has no Azure role assignments on any subscription or management group. She needs to assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope. In the Azure portal she browses to Microsoft Entra ID > Manage > Properties and sets the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, then signs out and signs back in. Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. Setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes assigns Anna the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/).
2. The elevated access is a global tenant property, so every user assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID gains the same access.
3. After elevating access, Anna can assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope.
opzione_a: Setting the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes assigns Anna the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/).
opzione_b: The elevated access is a global tenant property, so every user assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID gains the same access.
opzione_c: After elevating access, Anna can assign the Owner role to a security group at the root management group scope.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. Microsoft Learn states that when you set the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, you are assigned the User Access Administrator role in Azure RBAC at root scope (/), which grants permission to assign roles in all Azure subscriptions and management groups associated with the tenant. The toggle is only available to users assigned the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID. Statement 2 - No. The documentation is explicit that this setting is not a global property and applies only to the currently signed-in user; you can't elevate access for all members of the Global Administrator role. Each Global Administrator who needs elevated access must set the toggle individually. Statement 3 - Yes. The User Access Administrator role includes Microsoft.Authorization/*, so once elevated at root scope Anna can assign any Azure role, including Owner, at the root management group. Microsoft also documents that after the tenant administrator elevates access, the administrator can assign any Azure role to other directory users or groups to manage the hierarchy. Note that Microsoft recommends removing the elevated access (setting the toggle back to No) once the required changes at root scope are complete.
tags: elevate access, root management group, user access administrator, global administrator, entra id, rbac

domanda: The FinOps team at Litware creates a budget scoped to a management group named MG-Production and wants the budget to invoke an Azure Function through an action group when 80 percent of the budget amount is reached. While configuring the budget, the option to select an action group is not available. You need to enable the automation with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Re-create the budget at a subscription scope, because action groups are supported only for subscription and resource group budget scopes.
opzione_b: Assign the Cost Management Contributor role to the FinOps team at the MG-Production management group scope.
opzione_c: Enable the common alert schema on the action group so that budgets can integrate with it.
opzione_d: Change the budget alert type from actual cost to forecasted cost, because only forecasted alerts can trigger action groups.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Budgets can be created at the management group, subscription, and resource group scopes, but Microsoft Learn states that when you create or edit a budget for a subscription or resource group scope you can configure it to call an action group, and that action groups are currently only supported for subscription and resource group scopes. Moving the budget down to a subscription scope is therefore the required change. Wrong: b - this is a permissions role, and lack of permission is not why the control is hidden. Cost Management Contributor lets a user create and modify budgets, but no role makes action groups available at management group scope. Wrong: c - the documentation states you can integrate budgets with action groups regardless of whether the common alert schema is enabled or disabled in those groups, so the schema setting is irrelevant here. Wrong: d - both actual cost and forecasted cost budget alerts exist, and the alert type has no bearing on action group support; the limitation is the budget's scope.
tags: cost management, budgets, action groups, management group, scope, automation

domanda: You are briefing a new cloud administrator on how Microsoft Cost Management budgets behave. Which statements about budgets are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A budget can be created at the management group, subscription, or resource group scope.
opzione_b: A single budget supports up to five cost thresholds and up to five email recipients.
opzione_c: A budget scoped to a subscription or a resource group can be configured to trigger an action group when a threshold is met.
opzione_d: When the budget amount is exceeded, Azure automatically stops the resources within the budget scope to prevent further charges.
opzione_e: Budgets support only actual cost alerts; to alert on projected spending you must create a separate Azure Monitor metric alert rule.
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, c. (a) Microsoft Learn lists the supported Azure RBAC budget scopes as management group, subscription, and resource group (plus EA and Microsoft Customer Agreement billing scopes). (b) Budgets require at least one cost threshold and a corresponding email address, and you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget. (c) When you create or edit a budget for a subscription or resource group scope, you can configure it to call an action group, which can then run automation such as an Azure Function or a webhook. Wrong: d - this is the single most common misconception about budgets. The documentation states that notifications are triggered when the budget thresholds are exceeded, but resources aren't affected and your consumption isn't stopped. Budgets are an alerting and accountability tool, not an enforcement tool. Wrong: e - budgets natively support both actual cost alerts and forecasted cost alerts; you toggle between them with the Type field when configuring the alert, and forecasted alerts fire when the forecasted cost projection exceeds the set threshold. No separate Azure Monitor rule is needed.
tags: cost management, budgets, thresholds, forecasted alerts, action groups, scopes

domanda: Your organization uses an Enterprise Agreement and has purchased Azure Prepayment. You are documenting how Cost Management alerts behave so that the finance team knows what is automatic and what must be configured. Select the correct value for each statement.
opzione_a: Automatic thresholds at which credit alerts are generated: [50% and 75% | 80% and 100% | 90% and 100%]
opzione_b: Alert type that is supported for Enterprise Agreement but NOT for Microsoft Customer Agreement or pay-as-you-go: [Budget alert | Credit alert | Cost anomaly alert]
opzione_c: Maximum number of email recipients that can be configured in a single budget: [3 | 5 | 10]
opzione_d: Alert conditions you can configure on a budget: [Actual cost only | Forecasted cost only | Actual cost and forecasted cost]
risposta_corretta: 90% and 100%,Credit alert,5,Actual cost and forecasted cost
spiegazione: Correct values: 90% and 100% / Credit alert / 5 / Actual cost and forecasted cost. Microsoft Learn states that credit alerts notify you when your Azure Prepayment is consumed and are generated automatically at 90% and at 100% of your Azure Prepayment credit balance, and that Azure Prepayment is for organizations with Enterprise Agreements. The supported alert features table shows Credit and Department spending quota alerts are supported for Enterprise Agreement only, whereas Budget alerts are supported for Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement, and Web direct/Pay-As-You-Go. The budgets tutorial states you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget, and that you configure both actual cost and forecasted budget alerts, switching between them with the Type field. Wrong values: 50%/75% and 80%/100% are not the documented credit alert thresholds (50% or 75% are cited only as examples of department spending quota thresholds, which are configured, not automatic). Budget alerts are available across all three offer types, so they are not EA-exclusive; cost anomaly alerts are a separate, opt-in feature. 3 and 10 contradict the documented maximum of five email recipients. 'Actual cost only' and 'Forecasted cost only' each omit a supported alert type.
tags: cost management, cost alerts, credit alerts, azure prepayment, enterprise agreement, budgets

domanda:
Contoso is divesting a business unit. A pay-as-you-go subscription named Sub-BU must be handed over to the acquiring company, whose Azure account lives in a different Microsoft Entra tenant. In the Azure portal, an administrator opens the subscription, selects Transfer billing ownership, enters the recipient's email address, and selects the 'Move subscription tenant' option before sending the request. Evaluate each of the following statements:
1. Because 'Move subscription tenant' is selected, all existing Azure role assignments that grant access to resources in Sub-BU are permanently removed when the transfer completes.
2. The transfer request remains valid indefinitely until the recipient accepts or declines it.
3. Any user who holds the Owner role on Sub-BU can initiate the transfer of billing ownership.
opzione_a: Because 'Move subscription tenant' is selected, all existing Azure role assignments that grant access to resources in Sub-BU are permanently removed when the transfer completes.
opzione_b: The transfer request remains valid indefinitely until the recipient accepts or declines it.
opzione_c: Any user who holds the Owner role on Sub-BU can initiate the transfer of billing ownership.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. Microsoft Learn warns that if you choose to move the subscription to the new account's Microsoft Entra tenant, all Azure role assignments to access resources in the subscription are permanently removed, and only the user in the new account who accepts the transfer request will have access to manage the resources. The alternative is to clear the 'Move subscription tenant' option, which transfers billing ownership while maintaining existing Azure role assignments. Statement 2 - No. The documentation states that only one transfer request is active at a time and that a transfer request is valid for 15 days, after which it expires. Statement 3 - No. This conflates billing administration with Azure RBAC. The documentation states that only the account administrator of an account can transfer ownership of a subscription. The Owner role is an Azure RBAC role that controls access to resources in the subscription; it does not confer billing ownership rights. (For a Microsoft Azure plan subscription, you instead need to be an owner or contributor on the invoice section to which the subscription is billed.)
tags: subscription transfer, billing ownership, account administrator, entra tenant, rbac, pay-as-you-go

domanda: Case study: Litware, Inc. holds an Enterprise Agreement with Azure Prepayment. Azure spend is spread across 12 subscriptions organized under a management group named MG-Litware. The finance controller reports that the engineering subscription named Sub-Eng repeatedly overruns its allocated monthly spend, and the overrun is only discovered after the invoice arrives. Litware's requirements are: the finance mailbox must be notified before the monthly spend for Sub-Eng is projected to exceed 50,000 USD; no running workload may be stopped or throttled as a result of the notification; and the solution must require the least administrative effort. You need to recommend a solution. What should you configure?
opzione_a: A budget scoped to Sub-Eng with a monthly reset period and a forecasted cost alert that notifies the finance mailbox.
opzione_b: A credit alert on the Enterprise Agreement billing account, configured to fire when spending is projected to exceed 50,000 USD.
opzione_c: An Azure Advisor cost recommendation with an alert configured on the Cost category for Sub-Eng.
opzione_d: An Azure spending limit of 50,000 USD on Sub-Eng.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Budgets are supported at the subscription scope, and Microsoft Learn states that forecasted alerts provide advanced notification that your spending trends are likely to exceed your budget, generating alerts when the forecasted cost projection exceeds the set threshold. A monthly reset period matches the monthly requirement, and email recipients are configured directly on the budget's alert conditions. Critically, this meets the 'no workload may be stopped' requirement: the documentation states that when budget thresholds are exceeded, resources aren't affected and your consumption isn't stopped. Wrong: b - credit alerts notify you when your Azure Prepayment is consumed and are generated automatically at 90% and 100% of the prepayment credit balance. They are not configurable to an arbitrary currency amount, they are not forecast-based, they are scoped to the prepayment balance rather than to a single subscription, and they are sent to account owners rather than an arbitrary recipient list. Wrong: c - Azure Advisor's Cost category recommends optimizations such as right-sizing or shutting down underutilized virtual machines. It analyzes resource configuration and usage telemetry to suggest savings; it does not track spend against a monetary threshold and cannot notify anyone that a projected monthly spend will exceed 50,000 USD. Wrong: d - the Azure spending limit is not available on Enterprise Agreement subscriptions, cannot be set to a custom amount, and would violate the requirement that no workload be stopped, because reaching a spending limit disables deployed resources for the remainder of the billing period.
tags: cost management, budgets, forecasted alert, azure advisor, credit alert, spending limit, enterprise agreement
